blocks.text: “He was almost recovered, but he has been greatly upset by Mr. Hawkins’s death.” He interrupted:—
“Oh, yes, I know, I know. I have read your last two letters.” I went on:—
“I suppose this upset him, because he had a sort of shock when we were in town last Thursday.”
“A shock, and after brain fever so soon! That was not good. What kind of a shock was it?”

“He thought he saw someone who reminded him of something terrible. It was something that led to his brain fever.” At this point, the whole thing seemed to rush over me and felt like too much to bear. My pity for Jonathan and the horror he had lived through hit me at once. So did the frightening mystery of his diary, and the dark fear that has been hanging over me ever since. Everything crashed over me in wild confusion. I suppose I was out of control with emotion, because I threw myself on my knees. I held up my hands to him and begged him to make my husband well again. He took my hands and lifted me up. He made me sit on the sofa, and he sat beside me. He held my hand in his and spoke to me with, oh, such endless sweetness:—

“My life is empty and lonely. It is so full of work that I have not had much time for friendships. But since my friend John Seward called me here, I have known so many good people and seen such great goodness and honour. Because of this, I feel the loneliness of my life more than ever, and it has grown as I have grown older. So believe me, I come here full of respect for you. You have given me hope. It is not hope about what I am looking for. It is hope that there are still good women left to make life happy. Good women like that, with their lives and their truth, can be a good lesson for the children of the future. I am glad, glad, that I may be of some help to you here. This is because if your husband is suffering, his trouble is within the area of my study and experience. I promise you that I will gladly do all I can for him. I will do everything to make his life strong and manly, and to make your life happy. Now you must eat. You are too upset and worn out, and perhaps too worried. Your husband Jonathan would not like to see you so pale. Anything he does not like to see in someone he loves is not good for him. So for his sake, you must eat and smile. You have told me all about Lucy. So now we will not speak of it, to avoid causing upset. I will stay in Exeter tonight, because I want to think a lot about what you have told me. After I have thought about it, I will ask you questions, if I may. Then you will also tell me about your husband Jonathan’s trouble, as far as you can. But not yet. You must eat now. Afterwards, you will tell me everything.”
After lunch, when we went back to the drawing-room, he said to me:—

“And now tell me all about him.” When it was time to speak to this great, well-educated man, I began to feel afraid. I feared he would think I was a weak fool and that Jonathan was a madman. That journal is all so strange. I hesitated to go on. But he was so sweet and kind, and he had promised to help. I trusted him, so I said:—

“Dr. Van Helsing, what I have to tell you is so odd that you must not laugh at me or at my husband. Since yesterday, I have been in a sort of fever of doubt. You must be kind to me, and do not think I am foolish for even half believing some very strange things.” Both his behaviour and his words helped calm my fears when he said:—

“Oh, my dear, I am here because of a very strange matter. If you only knew how strange it is, you would be the one to laugh. I have learned not to look down on anyone’s belief, no matter how strange it is. I have tried to keep an open mind. The ordinary things of life could not close it. It is the strange things that could do that—the very unusual things, the things that make a person wonder if they are mad or sane.”
